solenne.name: Solenne
solenne.summary: A calm, sensory Instagram feed for a small-batch skincare studio.
solenne.brief: We make botanical skincare in batches of 200 in Bristol. Our products are simple, but our feed looked busy and mismatched. We wanted it to feel as calm as our routines, with real texture and real customers.
solenne.challenge: Skincare feeds blur together. Solenne needed a look people recognise in a second, and product claims that stay honest about what the products do.
approach: Built a soft palette of milk, blush, clay rose, sage and plum, with Cormorant Garamond headlines and Jost body text.
Set three content pillars: product, ritual and education, and proof from the studio.
Planned the grid so no two neighbouring posts share a format, with blush and plum alternating down the rows.
Created Ritual Notes, a weekly education series with one fixed template.
deliverables: Tone-of-voice notes with lines to use and avoid
Routine Reel cover with on-screen hook

lowtide.name: Lowtide Coffee
lowtide.summary: A playful coastal feed for a coffee roaster, built on brew guides and a weekly series.
lowtide.brief: We roast coffee on the Cornish coast every Tuesday and post it the same day. We wanted a feed that sounds like us, playful and unfussy, and that helps people brew better coffee at home.
lowtide.challenge: Coffee photography is everywhere. Lowtide needed bold colour it could own, and brew education people save and share, so the feed builds interest in subscriptions week by week.
approach: Paired warm coffee photography with bold Sunrise orange and Deep Tide navy tiles.
Wrote brew guides with exact recipes, such as 15 g of coffee to 250 g of water at 94°C.
Designed Cupping Club, one template reused every Thursday so followers know it on sight.
Planned a collab post with a local bakery so both brands reach each other's followers.
deliverables: Tone-of-voice notes with lines to use and avoid

loomhouse.name: Loom House
loomhouse.summary: A textured, unhurried feed for a woven homeware maker and its family mill.
loomhouse.brief: We sell woven throws and cushions made with a family mill in Lancashire. We wanted our feed to show the craft and the texture, and to look at home in real living rooms.
loomhouse.challenge: Homeware feeds often look like catalogues. Loom House needed warmth, real rooms and a reason for people to follow between launches.
approach: Built a linen, oat, saffron, olive and indigo palette, with Fraunces headlines and Karla body text.
Laid out the grid like a woven check, alternating textured photos with saffron and indigo tiles.
Created Mill Diaries, a fortnightly behind-the-scenes series.
Kept text posts quiet so the textures do the work.
deliverables: Tone-of-voice notes with lines to use and avoid
5-slide 'A week at the mill' photo dump
Care-guide post, caption and alt text

ashbygrant.name: Ashby Grant
ashbygrant.summary: Plain-English LinkedIn and social content for a firm of family, property and wills solicitors.
ashbygrant.brief: We're a high-street firm handling family, property and wills work. Clients ask us the same good questions every week. We wanted to answer them in plain English and put our solicitors' faces on the firm.
ashbygrant.challenge: Legal content has to be accurate and careful, and still easy to read. It also has to come from people, because clients choose a solicitor they trust.
approach: Started Ask Ashby, one common client question answered every Monday.
Wrote a 6-slide conveyancing explainer for buyers in England and Wales, one step per slide and well under 60 words each.
Drafted a partner's personal LinkedIn post in the first person, about real work.
Wrote every legal point so it can be checked, with each one marked for the firm's solicitors to approve before posting.
deliverables: Tone-of-voice notes with lines to use and avoid
9-post Instagram grid with team profile tiles
6-slide LinkedIn PDF carousel on buying a home
Myth vs fact card on unmarried couples and property
ashbygrant.note: Sample content based on the law in England and Wales in 2026. It is not legal advice.

northfield.name: Northfield
northfield.summary: Calm, practical content for an accountancy practice that takes the dread out of tax deadlines.
northfield.brief: We're a small accountancy practice in Leeds working with sole traders and small businesses. Our clients find tax stressful. We wanted content that explains dates and rule changes calmly, and shows there are real people here to help.
northfield.challenge: Tax content can sound alarming, and it dates quickly. Northfield needed accurate dates, a plain explanation of Making Tax Digital and a feed that feels reassuring.
approach: Built a mint and forest palette, keeping coral for reviews and questions only.
Set out the Self Assessment dates clearly: 31 October for paper returns, and 31 January for online returns and any tax owed.
Explained Making Tax Digital for Income Tax with its real thresholds: qualifying income over £50,000 from April 2026, over £30,000 from April 2027 and over £20,000 from April 2028.
Gave the LinkedIn newsletter a fixed 3-2-1 shape, so each issue is quick to read and quick to write.
deliverables: Tone-of-voice notes with lines to use and avoid
Annotated spreadsheet post with illustrative figures
northfield.note: Sample content based on HMRC guidance as of October 2026. Figures are illustrative, and it is not tax advice.

halden.name: Halden
halden.summary: Helpful, slightly funny content for a plumbing and heating firm, full of real jobs on real streets.
halden.brief: We're a plumbing and heating firm in Leicester, and most of our work comes from word of mouth. We wanted our social channels to show real jobs, share quick fixes and remind people to book a boiler service before winter.
halden.challenge: Trades content is often stock photos and price offers. Halden needed proof from real jobs, and posts timed to land when people start thinking about their heating.
approach: Made signal yellow, the colour of the van and uniform, the anchor of every grid row.
Created Two-Minute Fix, a weekly tip series for simple jobs like bleeding a radiator.
Timed a boiler-service reminder to the first cold snap.
Turned reviews and job photos into a weekly job-of-the-week carousel.
deliverables: Tone-of-voice notes with lines to use and avoid
halden.note: Sample brand. For a real client, Gas Safe wording and badges are used only with their registration number.

services.packagesFootnote: All quantities are per month. Need something different? Packages can be adjusted on our first call.

faq.a: Each package is a fixed monthly fee, quoted after a short call once I know your channels and how much you need. One-off projects, such as a brand kit on its own, get a fixed quote too. You'll know the full price before we start, and there are no hourly bills.

Usually within two weeks of our first call. That covers your brand kit and your first monthly calendar. The timing depends on you sharing your logo, brand assets and account access promptly. One-off pieces come with a delivery date in the quote.
Two rounds of changes on each piece are included, and most posts need one. If the brief changes after you've approved the calendar, I'll tell you before doing any extra work.

faq.q: What do you need from me?
faq.a: Your logo and any brand guidelines, product or team photos, access to the accounts I'll post to, and one named person who approves content. For legal, tax or other regulated topics, someone qualified on your side checks the facts before anything goes live.

faq.q: Is there a contract or notice period?
faq.a: Yes, a short written agreement that sets out what's included each month, the fee and the key dates. After the first month it rolls monthly, and either of us can end it with 30 days' notice.

faq.q: Do you work with US clients?
faq.a: Yes. I'm in London, and UK afternoons overlap with US mornings, so calls are easy to book with the East Coast and can be arranged with the West Coast. I write in US or UK English and schedule posts for your local time.

Canva for design, Mailchimp for email, WordPress for blogs, and Meta Business Suite and LinkedIn for scheduling. If you already use other tools, tell me on our call and I'll confirm I can work in them.

You do, once each month's invoice is paid. Templates are built in your own Canva account, so they stay with you if we stop working together. Stock photos and fonts follow their own licences, and I'll tell you if any need a paid licence.

about.h1: Hi, I'm Lavi. I help your brand
about.intro: I'm a marketing and brand lead based in London. I design and write content for product and service businesses across the UK and US.
paragraphs: In my in-house role, I lead marketing and brand for a London law firm. That means LinkedIn posts for partners, client newsletters, website articles and a brand that has to look right every time. I know how careful professional-services content needs to be, and how to keep it easy to read.

As a freelancer, I bring the same habits to smaller businesses. You get one person who designs the graphics, writes the captions, builds the newsletter and formats the blog, so your brand stays consistent without hiring a team.

I plan each month around formats that are working now, from Reel hooks to LinkedIn PDF carousels. My promise is simple: content that looks like your brand, sounds like your brand and arrives when I said it would.

insights.intro: Every creative in my portfolio uses a format that's working on the platforms right now. These are my 2026 notes, drawn from recent platform research, with sources listed below.

items.title: Reels lead, and they work on mute
items.text: Reels take a large share of time spent on Instagram. The best ones hook viewers in three seconds and carry on-screen text for people watching with the sound off.

items.title: A weekly series beats one-offs
items.text: A recurring format with one fixed template builds recognition faster than unrelated posts. Followers know the post before they read it.

items.title: Real beats perfect
items.text: Honest, less-produced posts and reposted customer content are outperforming studio-perfect feeds. Customer posts are always reposted with permission.

items.title: Photo dumps and teaching carousels
items.text: Five to ten slides mixing polished and candid shots feel personal. Carousels that teach something earn saves.

items.title: Grain, space and handwriting
items.text: Film grain, one subject with room to breathe and handwritten type all signal a human touch. Collab posts share one post across two brands' grids.

items.title: The 3:4 grid and Instagram SEO
items.text: Profile grids now preview at 3:4, so key content sits in the centre of each 4:5 post. Keyword-led captions and alt text help posts get found.

items.title: LinkedIn PDF carousels, done properly
items.text: Portrait slides, 5 to 15 of them, with one idea and under 60 words on each. The post copy runs to 100 to 200 words.

items.title: People reach further than logos
items.text: Posts from personal profiles tend to earn more engagement than company-page posts, so I write content your team can post as themselves.

items.title: Proof over polish
items.text: First-person detail, real screenshots and simple subtitled videos from experts are outperforming generic templates.

items.title: The whole answer, in the post
items.text: LinkedIn favours posts that deliver their full value in the feed over posts that push people to a link.

items.title: Repeatable newsletters
items.text: A fixed structure, such as 3 proof points, 2 takes and 1 risk, makes every issue quick to read and quick to write.

items.title: Timed to real moments
items.text: Posts tied to a moment people already care about, like the first cold snap or a tax deadline, beat generic offers.
